title: Keeping blood glucose in range
objective: Explain how insulin and glucagon keep blood glucose near a set point.

steps.title: Two hormones, opposite jobs
steps.body:
**[[blood glucose]]** is held in a narrow range by a push-pull pair:

- After a meal, glucose rises → **[[insulin]]** tells liver, muscle and fat to take glucose up → glucose falls.
- When fasting, glucose drops → **[[glucagon]]** tells the liver to release glucose → glucose rises.

It's a classic balancing loop around a **[[set point]]**.

visual.alt: Blood glucose plotted over time around a set point, with insulin and glucagon bars. After a meal glucose rises, insulin rises and glucose falls back. During a fast glucose dips, glucagon rises and glucose settles near the set point. With the hormones switched off, glucose drifts far from the set point.
visual.caption: Insulin and glucagon push glucose back toward the set point. Try a meal, a fast, then switch the hormones off.

steps.prompt: Blood glucose rises after a meal. Which hormone responds, and what does it do?
options: Insulin — drives glucose into cells, lowering it
Glucagon — releases more glucose, raising it
Somatostatin — boosts insulin release, lowering it
Glucagon — stores glucose as glycogen, lowering it
steps.explanation: High glucose → β cells release insulin → tissues take up glucose → glucose returns toward the set point.

variants.setup: You've just eaten and blood glucose spikes.
variants.prompt: Which hormone brings it back down?
variants.reveal: Insulin drives glucose uptake, lowering it back toward the set point.

steps.setup: A person hasn't eaten for 12 hours and blood glucose starts to fall.
options: Insulin rises to lower it further
Glucagon rises and the liver releases glucose
Nothing changes until the next meal
steps.reveal: Falling glucose triggers glucagon from α cells; the liver releases stored glucose, nudging it back up. The two hormones work against each other to hold the set point.

variants.prompt: During fasting, blood glucose is kept up mainly by…
variants.explanation: Glucagon prompts hepatic glucose release during fasting.

steps.title: A feedback loop
steps.body: This is **[[negative feedback]]**: the output (glucose) feeds back to adjust the hormones that control it. The next unit (D8) makes this loop logic explicit — it's the backbone of physiology.

reviewNotes: Glucose regulation as negative feedback; forward-ref to D8.
